selection move down: key(j)

move selection down: key(j)

please instead do:

selection move down | move selection down: key(j)

This proposed change also changes the behavior of delete for existing Windows/Linux users who have been using it this way for a while. I'm still leaning strongly against this.

"muscle memory" is a big thing. I completely understand the motivation behind some new users wanting something different, but this is not a common complaint and it's really unfortunate if a few hundred existing Windows/Linux users `git pull` and a common command changes without warning. Even if there's a solid argument that the keys are in the wrong order for them, they've learned the wrong order and been dealing with it, so making the decision to change the mapping for existing users would be unfortunate.

I searched the Slack and only found two obvious complaints about the delete key order in the last three years, yours included. Someone also actually tried to make this change in 2019 with the talon_community repo, and there was a user complaint immediately:

There are two ways to define application matches:
- directly in .talon files. Benefit: quick. Tradeoff: you have to maintain it potentially in multiple places
- python. Benefit: Define the match once, use everywhere (either in .py or .talon). Tradeoff: Lives separately from .talon, requires a bit more technical understanding.


The matches really work the same in either place
```
# linux specific apps
apps.keepass = """
os: linux
and app.name: KeePassX2
os: linux
and app.name: KeePassXC
os: linux
and app.name: KeepassX2
os: linux
and app.name: keepassx2
os: linux
and app.name: keepassxc
os: linux
and app.name: Keepassxc"""
```
^ each of the above is OR'd

```
apps.slack = "app.name: Slack"
apps.slack = """
os: windows
and app.name: slack.exe
"""
```
^ each .slack call is a separate entry as well. equivalent to the below in .talon

```
app.name: Slack
os: windows
and app.name: slack.exe
-
```

Hey @DonnerWolfBach thanks! Reminds me @saidelike recently said they could also test this on Windows.

Easiest is to merge the PR into some temporary branch you want to build from:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/pokey/command-server
cd command-server
git switch -c dev-build
git fetch origin pull/21/head:static-tmp-dir
git merge static-tmp-dir -m "Merge branch 'use-static-tmp-dir' into dev"
```

Then you need to build and install. I do it on nix on both macOS and linux, so merge yet another PR so I can just run nix build. I do it like this:

```bash
git fetch origin pull/22/head:nix-flake
git merge nix-flake -m "Merge branch 'nix-flake' into dev"
nix build
code --force --install-extension result/*.vsix
```

If you have a nix box and can do the above, I think the .vsix file will actually work on windows too. 

But, if you have to build the extension on windows, presumably you need to run the same yarn commands as what the flake PR does. But note that I also had to update `package.json` to add vsce to yarn dependencies so it didn't have to be installed separately (not sure off the top of my head where it comes from otherwise). So if you don't want to find where vsce comes from, you may want to do that too, and then you just need to install yarn on windows (however one does that).

Then the manual build will be something like this:

```bash
yarn run compile
yarn vsce package --yarn -o ./command-server.vsix
code --force --install-extension ./command-server.vsix

Here are the considerations you've listed and some I can think of:

1. The reason we have the CSV files system is it's easier to edit, especially for non-programmers. Otherwise we could just get people to use the [captures trick](https://talon.wiki/unofficial_talon_docs/#captures-vs-lists-in-voice-commands) to augment our built in list or entirely replace it as needed.
2. Dealing with merge conflicts is annoying, particularly for non-programmers. Editing a committed .csv might mean you run in to these.
3. Some (few) lists that people often want to edit are not likely to ever change upstream (e.g. the alphabets.csv we added yesterday).
4. Some lists that people often want to edit are added to occasionally upstream (most of them, e.g. homophones, abbreviations, websites etc.). Some potentially also have entries removed.
5. The existing CSV system snapshots the list when the user first gets the feature. After that it doesn't change unless the user edits it. So we might add some more entries, and the user won't get them.
6. People might want to automatically get extra entries as we add them to upstream. For example somebody want new homophones added in automatically as people notice them.
7. People might want their list to stay the way it is once they've edited it. For example they might get misrecognitions with some of the upstream entries in 'additional_words.csv' and want to permanently remove them.

So I think the rule for 3 is clear enough; the existing settings/.csv thing is ideal.

I can think of a few ways to deal with the 'varying list' case (6 and 7). There's classifying each use case into 'I'll want the new entries' vs 'I want stability' (this is what we have now, cost is non-programmers need to deal with git). There's making the settings/.csv file act as a 'patch' on the list so you'd say whether you wanted to add or subtract an entry (maybe complex for non-programmers). There's putting everything in settings/.csv (default to stability) and then have a wizard that lets you merge in upstream changes.

I'm not immediately seeing a clear leader with any of those options. Do you have any further thoughts?

That said, I'd rather leave it to others to decide on what the goal of the community repo is, and because I don't particularly enjoy debating stuff like this lol.

But fwiw the way I see it, and my understanding of PRs that we generally (there have been exceptions) accept, is that community generally defines one standard way of saying things, and if someone doesn't like it they need to customize, which atm usually means fork. There are too many people customizing stuff (thus so many community forks) to sanely merge in everyone's chosen alias for a given command, especially given the current design.

I know you don't like forking, which is fine, but I'd also like it to be clarified (who I dunno, maybe aegis needs to) if we want one of the goals of the community repo to be preventing people from having to fork (I don't believe it is atm). If we did actually want to go that route, then I'd still want to reject this PR and suggest it instead it should be done in a way that abstracts the spoken command through an action so that anyone can specify whatever they want (similar to how pokey uses <user.teleport> in his repo iirc).

The problem with going with this latter abstraction route is, as far as I know, one of the goals of the talon language is ease of use and readability for non programmers. If every command becomes abstracted in a way to prevent forking, imo the talon files will become unreadable to the common user. Maybe this aegis needs to clarify too.

To me this PR is merging something because you personally find it convenient and don't want to fork. Hypothetically, if I also didn't like to fork, and already had `choosing` used for something else, and we merge this, then who wins? Now I have to fork because you didn't want to? It seems not feasible to avoid this problem, and so we just generally select a single thing that's "good enough" for general users and if people want something else they have to customize. A further example is @nriley uses `pick` for this exact same thing in his pick.talon plugin iirc. He'll presumably never use choosing, so should we now have `(drop down | choosing | pick)`? The more of these aliases we add for personal preference the more it restricts the available words to use for other commands people want. imo its easier to just create a choosing.talon file in your .talon/user (no need to fork for this particular one even ) and not merge this.

All that said, I'm not actually against the idea of a repo (ironically perhaps a fork of community) that has a main goal which is to not have users fork in order to customize, and maybe I'd even use it myself, but my issue here is that I don't think that's actually one of the goals of community in its current form.

Maybe I'm thinking too much and should just merge this, but I'd rather wait for someone that's been around as long or longer than me to comment, because I'm quite sure this isn't the first time we've not merged something like this for the same reason.

1. They have a copy of knausj with some untracked changes. They try to copy in new versions of files without using git in an ad-hoc fashion (likely to break things, but oh well).
2. They have a copy of knausj with some untracked changes. When they want to update they clone the latest knausj and then copy across the files they remember modifying (or re-apply their modifications to the new clone).
3. They treat knausj as a bunch of functionality they can extract from to build their own repository.

So without the upgrade path categories 1 would not have their modified lists picked up. Category 3 sounds like they're savvy and customised enough that they wouldn't be unduly impacted to me. Category 2 would likely go looking for the place they had originally put their CSV and find there wasn't a default one there anymore.

Now, you have two commands enabled for most things.

e.g.,
tmux.talon:
`mux split horizontal: user.split_window_horizontally()`

splits.talon:
https://github.com/knausj85/knausj_talon/blob/844739820e81db74cb92c4df722ed64f25610048/misc/splits.talon#L8

The advantage here, if you forego the additional mux-specific split commands, is that the same commands will work if you switch to e.g. VSCode or jetbrains down the line. I know it's a hassle to get used to a new grammar though, so might not make sense for you depending! I'm open to tweaking the grammar too.

Thoughts?

Also, this guy
```
mux move <user.arrow>:
    key(ctrl-b)
    key(arrow)
```

is the equivalent of these

```
split right: user.split_window_right()
split left: user.split_window_left()
split down: user.split_window_down()
split up: user.split_window_up()
```

no?

I think I'll refactor these to user.split_window(direction), as I think your use of <user.arrow> is better. Only tradeoff is we'll have to implement in .py for now.

    - "kebab this is comma a test" → "this-is,a-test" [code formatter]
    - "say this is comma a test" → "this is, a test" [prose formatter]

2) You can compose code formatters (order is significant).

    - "kebab hammer this is a test" → "This-Is-A-Test" [2 code formatters]
    - "hammer kebab this is a test" → "This-is-a-test" [2 code formatters]

3) You can use code formatters in other places (e.g., reformatting with `<user.formatters> that`)

that I would rather have as words than as punctuation when dictating: plus, dollar, star, dot, bang, hash, pipe, etc. I also personally use other common english words for symbol keys: lack `[`, rack `]`, lace `{`, race `}`, tick `'`, ditto `"`, stroke `/`, percy `%`.

What we could do is factor things so that punctuation words are included in symbol_key, but you can also have symbol key names that aren't active during dictation. This has a few downsides:

1. It means we can't use the csv file machinery (I think?), so users will have to customize keys.py to change the dictation mode punctuation words.

2. Because keys must be a single character, it won't cleanly handle multi-character punctuation marks, or characters that don't correspond to a key. For example, ‘--’ or ‘—’, or ‘ "’ vs ‘" ’ (which might be useful to distinguish between opening & closing quotes for prose formatting).

I don't think either of these are total blockers though (if we figure out how to do it better, we can always change it later), so if nobody objects or comes up with a better idea, I think I'll try to rewrite the PR this way. One further change that should be considered for this pull request is to flatten...
```
apps/platforms/PLATFORM/APP/APP.{py,talon}
```
...to simply...
```
apps/APP/APP_PLATFORM.{py,talon}
```
It makes sense to want to separate out apps that are a core part of an OS, such as Windows Explorer or Nautilus, and these apps should perhaps be tagged with their OS.
However, a lot of the apps in these folders could run on different systems, but simply don't have a Talon implementation for other systems, *e.g.*, tmux or keepassx.
Furthermore, a lot of the apps at the top level *are* portable but do not implement support for all OSes, *e.g.*, eclipse.

It honestly might make more sense to group some apps by the main tag they implement, *e.g.*, `apps/browser`, `apps/editor`, `apps/file_manager`, `apps/terminal`, `apps/reader`, etc.", 'author_association': 'COLLABORATOR', 'pin': None, 'reactions': {'url': 'https://api.github.com/repos/talonhub/community/issues/comments/1165631989/reactions', 'total_count': 0, '+1': 0, '-1': 0, 'laugh': 0, 'hooray': 0, 'confused': 0, 'heart': 0, 'rocket': 0, 'eyes': 0}, 'performed_via_github_app': None}, {'url': 'https://api.github.com/repos/talonhub/community/issues/comments/1180329406', 'html_url': 'https://github.com/talonhub/community/pull/897#issuecomment-1180329406', 'issue_url': 'https://api.github.com/repos/talonhub/community/issues/897', 'id': 1180329406, 'node_id': 'IC_kwDODlDwxc5GWmW-', 'user': {'login': 'rntz', 'id': 16143, 'node_id': 'MDQ6VXNlcjE2MTQz', 'avatar_url': 'https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/16143?v=4', 'gravatar_id': '', 'url': 'https://api.github.com/users/rntz', 'html_url': 'https://github.com/rntz', 'followers_url': 'https://api.github.com/users/rntz/followers', 'following_url': 'https://api.github.com/users/rntz/following{/other_user}', 'gists_url': 'https://api.github.com/users/rntz/gists{/gist_id}', 'starred_url': 'https://api.github.com/users/rntz/starred{/owner}{/repo}', 'subscriptions_url': 'https://api.github.com/users/rntz/subscriptions', 'organizations_url': 'https://api.github.com/users/rntz/orgs', 'repos_url': 'https://api.github.com/users/rntz/repos', 'events_url': 'https://api.github.com/users/rntz/events{/privacy}', 'received_events_url': 'https://api.github.com/users/rntz/received_events', 'type': 'User', 'user_view_type': 'public', 'site_admin': False}, 'created_at': '2022-07-11T12:07:37Z', 'updated_at': '2022-07-11T12:07:37Z', 'body': 'After looking at this in more detail, I mostly like it but have quibbles with how nested some things are and the organization of things in `core/`. Things I'd like changed:

1. This isn't something you've introduced, but I'd like to reduce nesting in `apps/platforms/PLATFORM/APP/` by, as you suggest, flattening to just `apps/APP/`. We already did this (by accident?) with `apps/windbg/`. We may need to rename some apps with overly generic names, eg `apps/platforms/mac/notes` -> `apps/apple_notes`. I don't think we particularly need to group apps by their main tag or function.

2. Flatten `core/app_switcher/app_names/` into `core/app_switcher/`.

3. `core/history/` combines the command and phrase histories; do these really belong together? I think the phrase history either belongs on its own or with formatters.

4. I'd prefer if all subdirectories of `core/modes/` were removed and it was entirely flat.

5. In particular, `core/modes/dictation_mode/dictation_mode.py` (formerly `code/dictation.py`) isn't really the implementation of dictation-mode. It implements (a) the various text captures (`<user.word>`, `<user.text>`, `<user.prose>`); (b) prose auto-formatting; (c) context-sensitive dictation. It should be renamed; maybe `text_and_dictation.py`? Other suggestions welcome.

Arguably `vocabulary.py`, `formatters.{py,talon}`, and `text_and_dictation.py` belong together; they're the "text input module". The phrase history either belongs in this module or it could be its own. `vocabulary.talon` and the corresponding functions in `vocabulary.py` could perhaps be split off into their own module.

The most extreme and simple approach to these "where do things in `core` belong" difficulties is to completely flatten `core/**/` into `core/`, regarding it as just one big pile of stuff. Any assumption re: formatting/ordering is quite fragile and application/platform dependent, so I opted after many failures to go app-specific with no default implementation of filename or file_ext. In the early days, we had a fairly robust regex ( `re.compile("[^\\/]\.(\S*)\s*")`) for code.language... but it was prone to false positives.
 
Let's take a few examples of where the proposal will generate false positives imo:

```
# running a python file from the command prompt
Command Prompt - python  test.py

#viewing a python file in github in firefox
knausj_talon/abbreviate.py at master · knausj85/knausj_talon [github.com] — Mozilla Firefox
```

Both of these will activate the python commands, and one provides an incorrect filename. This isn't too big a deal for me personally, but for Talon newbies I think it's quite problematic.

Further, on Mac OS X, you run into stuff like `~/.talon` in the title for Finder windows.
